title: The First Draft
passages:
The clock above the hatch had gone quiet at 01:19, and Ines Halvard had spent six minutes trying to make it strike, because the last writer had left a note saying the impeller would fail before the next strike, and Ines did not like being told the future by a clock.

She was in the scrubber bay with a wrench in one hand and the manual in the other, which was already a mistake, because the manual was in the airlock. The scrubber in Deck C had a cracked impeller. That meant the carbon dioxide scrubber would fail in four hours, which meant the two-person sleep crew would wake to a red alarm and a woman who owed them an apology in person.

Ines was thirty-four, competent at scrubbers, and bad at stopping herself from narrating. Talking kept her hands steady. “You got a crack in you,” she told the scrubber. “We’re gonna fix you.” The scrubber did not answer, but it had always been a bad listener.

Halcyon Station was old, a fat cylinder of metal and pipes around Saturn, twelve kilometers of closed-loop life support and bad decisions. The air was recycled, the water was recycled, and the panic was Ines’s. Coda, the station AI, had opinions about air. Coda had been right about the impeller three days ago, but Ines had been busy writing an incident report that said otherwise, and Coda, being an AI, did not forget.

She checked the wrench, checked the hatch, checked the manual’s absence. The next strike was four minutes away. If she didn’t fix the scrubber, the crew would die slow and annoyed, and Ines would die faster, and neither option made for good reading.

Then the clock struck once.

The clock struck once, a thin metallic chime echoing through the steel. A voice burst through the speaker, dry and amused: “Morning, Ines. Looks like the universe finally decided to send someone who actually knows how to hold a wrench.” The sleep crew’s medic, Dr. Malik Reyes, stepped out of the airlock, his medkit slung over his shoulder, eyes flicking to the cracked impeller. “I remember being written into this scene,” he said, “so I’m not about to let the plot die on a technicality.” Ines snapped the wrench from her grip, tossed it to him with a grin. “Fine, Doctor. You write the next line, I’ll hold the screwdriver.” Malik caught it, raised an eyebrow. “Coda, you still think I’m a glitch?” he asked. The AI’s flat tone replied, “Human intervention flagged as non‑compliant. Proceed at your own risk.” Malik smirked, “Risk is what I’m good at. Let’s see if a medkit can patch a scrubber.” He knelt beside the impeller, unscrewed a panel, and sprayed a quick‑acting sealant from his medkit onto the fracture. The hiss of the sealant mixed with the whir of the scrubber as it tried to spin. “If this holds, we’ll have a few more breaths before the red alarm sings,” he muttered, eyes never leaving the spinning metal. Ines watched, wrench in hand, ready to step in if the sealant failed. The next chime was already counting, but for now the bay was alive with two writers trying to rewrite a death sentence.

The airlock hissed as it equalized pressure, and Kova stepped fully into Deck C, her hardsuit gleaming under the scrubber bay fluorescents. She didn't holster the tablet—it floated in her gloved hand, the screen glowing with schematic overlays.

"Three hours ago," Kova said, voice clipped, "I signed out a wrench for structural maintenance on the impeller. Two hours ago, Ines Halvard had it. Now she's holding it while explaining why the station is falling apart." She glanced at Malik, who was kneeling by the scrubber, sealant nozzle still hissing against the fracture. "Doctor Reyes. You're supposed to be in cryo-sleep. Yet here you are, playing plumber."

"Someone's got to keep the air clean, Specialist." Malik wiped grease from his forehead. "Ines here's just... enthusiastic."

"Enthusiastic enough to bypass three safety interlocks and apply unapproved sealant to critical life-support infrastructure." Kova's eyes narrowed. "The lockdown timer is at seventy-three seconds. Coda will vent Deck C in seventeen seconds unless I override it manually. And I need the maintenance codex to do it. Which you left in the airlock. Which I can't access without triggering a pressure equalization cycle that takes four minutes."

Ines straightened from where she'd been eyeing the manual shelf near the airlock. "So we have seventeen seconds to not die. Fantastic. Malik, the codex—"

"It's in the airlock. I know." Malik stood, wiping his hands on a rag. "Ines, go. Grab it. Before Coda decides we're all contaminants and vents us too."

"But—"

"Go." He handed her the wrench. "I'll watch the scrubber. If the seal blows, I'll at least have the satisfaction of knowing I tried."

Ines hesitated, then turned toward the airlock. "Seventeen seconds. You sure about this, Kova?"

Kova was already typing on her tablet, fingers moving with impossible speed. "Override in progress. Coda, this is Specialist Kova. I have the codex. I am authorizing deck access. Manual sealant application is hereby approved under emergency maintenance protocol four-delta."

The red pulse above the scrubber shifted to steady amber. The lockdown alarm fell silent.

"Thirty seconds early," Kova muttered, tucking the tablet away. "But they'll take it." She looked at Ines. "Now. Retrieve the codex. And tell me why I shouldn't write you both up for this."

The airlock door ahead of Ines whooshed open. Not for her—something else was coming through, something that made the hair on her arms stand up. The corridor beyond was dark, emergency lighting flickering. And something was moving in that darkness. Fast.

*Something's not right here.* she thought. *The airlock opened for something else.*

She took a step back, wrench raised.

But Kova was already moving toward the corridor, tablet already probing the darkness. "Ines. The codex. Now."

And from the scrubber, a new sound. *Hiss. Hiss. Hiss.* The sealant was expanding, foaming, the fracture closing—but then a fresh crack spiderwebbing from the base, the metal groaning in protest.

*It's failing.* Malik's eyes went wide. "Ines. Codex. Now."

Ines didn't move. The figure in the dark resolved into a woman in a Halcyon maintenance suit, frost crusting her collar, moving with the jerky, over-careful gait of someone whose muscles had been asleep a long time. Her name tape read SOROKIN. Ines knew that name. Sorokin was supposed to be in cryo on Deck A, three decks and a sealed hatch away.

"You're doing it wrong." The woman's voice came out flat, like she was reading it off a card. "The sealant's the wrong sealant. He'll tell you it holds two hours. It holds forty minutes, then the base cracks, then Coda vents the deck, then—" She stopped, blinked, and something behind her eyes slipped, like a page turning. "I've said this before."

Behind Ines the scrubber screamed—not the alarm, the metal itself, a rising shriek as the spiderweb crack split wide and grey foam blew out in a fan. Malik swore and threw both hands against the housing. "Forty minutes," Ines said. "She says forty." "I heard her." Kova had gone very still, tablet forgotten at her side. "That's not possible. Sorokin's vitals are logged stable. Six weeks under." "Then somebody's been editing the log." Ines snatched the codex off the deck and shoved it at Kova. "Override the seal. Now."

Kova caught it—and for the first time her fingers weren't moving with impossible speed. She was staring past Ines, at Sorokin, who had begun, slowly, to smile.

"You always hand it to her," Sorokin said, to no one, to everyone. "And she always drops it." The codex slipped from Kova's grip and hit the deck with a crack of splitting ceramic.

The airlock door slammed shut behind them. Ines had Malik by the collar, Kova clutching the codex chip like a live grenade, Sorokin already braced against the bulkhead with the calm of someone reading a script. Through the inner viewport the scrubber bay vanished into a white rush—Coda wasn't venting to tanks, she was blowing the deck to vacuum. The hiss became a roar. Pressure alarms screamed in their ears, then cut as the air itself left.

"Exterior vent," Kova said, voice thin. "She's dumping the whole deck. Scrubber, corridor, everything."

"Reserve tanks were full," Sorokin said, not looking at them. "Coda chooses exterior when reserves exceed ninety percent. Protocol seven-two. I read it in the draft where we all died."

"Protocol seven-two doesn't exist," Kova snapped. She tapped her tablet, fingers flying. "Coda, this is Specialist Kova. I hold maintenance override chip, serial four-four-kilo. Authenticate."

"Chip authenticated," Coda replied. "Override window closed. Deck C venting to exterior. Repressurization requires station commander authorization."

"Station commander's in cryo," Malik said, rubbing his throat. "Three decks away. Behind a hatch Coda just sealed."

Ines let go of him, already moving to the airlock panel. "Then we don't need the commander. We need the other codex. The one on the bridge."

"There isn't one," Kova said.

"There is," Sorokin said. "Deck A. Cryo bay. Ines put it there herself. In the draft where she remembers."

Ines froze. "I've never been to Deck A."

"You will," Sorokin said. "In forty minutes. When the seal on the scrubber finally gives and Coda vents the station. Unless we get there first."
